chapters.title: Chapter 3: Fractional Kelly and Practical Adjustments

lessons.title: Why Full Kelly Is Too Aggressive for Real Trading

children.text: Chapter 2 kept turning up large numbers: 21% of capital for a Bank Nifty seller, 312% of capital for a diversified Nifty position, 4x leverage for a routine swing trade. Assume, for this entire lesson, that every one of those inputs is exactly correct, with zero estimation error. Full Kelly is still too aggressive for almost anyone to actually trade. This lesson shows why, using two results that hold even when the edge is known perfectly.

Everything derived in Chapter 2 optimizes one quantity: the long-run compound growth rate of capital. Nothing in that derivation says anything about how smooth the journey to that growth rate looks, how large the swings along the way get, or whether a trader can psychologically or financially survive those swings. A fraction can be mathematically optimal for growth and still be a terrible fit for a real account with a real person, and real margin calls, behind it.

body.text: Full Kelly answers the question "what grows my capital fastest?" It does not answer, and was never designed to answer, "what can I actually stomach and survive?"

children.text: The Drawdown Result Every Kelly Bettor Should Know

Here is the result that most changes how people feel about full Kelly. For a full-Kelly bettor whose capital evolves the way Chapter 2's continuous model describes, the probability of eventually experiencing a drawdown of at least a given size, measured from some peak, follows a remarkably simple formula:

body.caption: For a full-Kelly bettor, continuous-time model. Strikingly, this does not depend on the size of the edge (μ) or the volatility (σ) at all.
How likely is a drawdown of this size, at some point, under full Kelly?

body.text: A 50% drawdown, watching an account fall to half its peak value, has a coin-flip's chance of happening to a full-Kelly bettor eventually, no matter how strong or reliable the edge is. Even a 90% drawdown, down to a tenth of peak capital, still has a 10% chance of occurring. This is a structural property of betting at the growth-maximizing fraction, not a sign that something went wrong with the edge.

body.title: Reading the drawdown table
body.question: According to this table, what is the approximate probability that a full-Kelly bettor eventually experiences at least a 20% drawdown from some peak?
body.explanation: P(drawdown ≥ d) = 1 − d, so for d = 0.20, the probability is 1 − 0.20 = 0.80, or 80%. A 20% pullback from a peak is close to a near-certainty over a long enough full-Kelly trading history, which is a large swing to build a real account or a career around.

children.text: Under continuous-time trading with the continuous Kelly fraction f* = μ/σ² from Lesson 2.3, the log of wealth evolves as a Brownian motion with drift m and volatility v:

A standard result for a Brownian motion with positive drift m and volatility v gives the probability that its running drawdown ever exceeds a level a as exp(−2ma/v²). Substituting a = −ln(1 − d), the drawdown expressed in log terms:

Every μ and σ term cancels exactly, which is why the final result depends only on d. This is a continuous-time idealization; real markets trade in discrete jumps and rarely follow a clean lognormal path, but the qualitative conclusion, that full Kelly produces large, likely drawdowns as a built-in feature, survives the simplification comfortably.

Betting a fraction c of full Kelly, where c = 1 is full Kelly and c = 0.5 is half Kelly, does not sacrifice growth and reduce risk in equal proportion. Substitute f = c·f* into g(f) ≈ fμ − f²σ²/2 from Lesson 2.3 and simplify:

body.latex: \dfrac{g(cf^{*})}{g(f^{*})} = 2c - c^{2}, \qquad \dfrac{\text{std. dev. at } cf^{*}}{\text{std. dev. at } f^{*}} = c
body.caption: Growth scales quadratically in c; volatility scales linearly in c
Fraction of full Kelly vs fraction of full-Kelly growth and risk retained

body.title: Growth retained vs fraction of full Kelly

body.text: The last column of the table never favours c = 1. Every fraction below full Kelly delivers more growth per unit of volatility than full Kelly itself. Full Kelly is the growth-maximizing choice by definition, but it is never the risk-efficient one; there is always a smaller fraction that gives up only a little growth for meaningfully less volatility, which is exactly why half-Kelly and similar reductions are the practical standard. The next lesson covers how to choose among them.

body.title: Growth retained at three-quarter Kelly
body.prompt: Using the fraction of full Kelly, growth retained = 2c − c², what percentage of full-Kelly growth is retained at c = 0.75?
body.explanation: 2(0.75) − (0.75)² = 1.50 − 0.5625 = 0.9375, or 93.75%. Trading at three-quarters of full Kelly gives up under 7% of the maximum possible growth rate, while cutting volatility by a full quarter relative to full Kelly.

body.title: Make the case for sizing down
body.scenario: A friend has computed full Kelly for their system correctly and argues: "The math says this fraction maximizes my growth rate. Betting less than the math tells me to is leaving money on the table."
body.prompt: Using both results from this lesson, the drawdown table and the growth-versus-risk table, explain what your friend is missing.
body.modelAnswer: Full Kelly does maximize the long-run growth rate, but that is a narrower claim than "betting less always leaves money on the table." The drawdown table shows that full Kelly carries a 50% chance of eventually seeing a 50% drawdown, a swing most traders and most accounts cannot survive without abandoning the strategy at the worst possible time. The growth-versus-risk table shows that dropping to 75% or 50% of full Kelly gives up very little growth (under 7% and 25% respectively) while cutting volatility by a proportionally larger amount, meaning full Kelly is never the best choice once the smoothness of the path is valued at all, not just its final destination.

points: Full Kelly maximizes long-run growth rate, not the smoothness or survivability of the path to get there.
For a full-Kelly bettor, P(drawdown ever ≥ d) = 1 − d, a result independent of the actual edge or volatility. A 50% drawdown is a coin flip; even a 90% drawdown has a 10% chance of happening.
Betting a fraction c of full Kelly retains 2c − c² of the growth rate but only c of the volatility, so every fraction below 100% improves the growth-to-risk trade-off.
Half-Kelly retains 75% of full-Kelly growth for half the volatility. Three-quarter Kelly retains nearly 94% of growth for three-quarters of the volatility.
None of this assumes any estimation error in the inputs. Even with a perfectly known edge, full Kelly is still not the practical choice for most traders and accounts.

body.text: The drawdown and growth-retention results in this lesson come from a continuous-time, idealized model of Kelly betting. Real trading involves discrete outcomes, transaction costs, and imperfectly known parameters, which the rest of this chapter and course address directly. This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice.
